title: Properties of electromagnetic waves 1
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: Properties of electromagnetic waves 1 — AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification, section 4.6.2.2.
meta_desc: GCSE Physics (AQA) practice covering Properties of electromagnetic waves 1, specification section 4.6.2.2.
final_note: You worked through Properties of electromagnetic waves 1 — 7 specification statements.

concepts.def: When a wave meets a substance and its energy is transferred into that substance instead of continuing through it. The wave does not emerge on the far side and the internal energy of the substance increases.

When a wave passes through a substance and emerges on the other side. A substance that transmits a wave lets it carry on, although the velocity of the wave inside the substance may differ from its velocity outside.

When a wave meets a boundary and travels back into the substance it came from rather than entering the new substance. Reflection is a third possibility alongside absorption and transmission, and in general all three happen at once in different proportions.

Whether a particular substance absorbs, transmits, refracts or reflects an electromagnetic wave is not a single fixed property of that substance: it varies with the wavelength of the wave. Glass transmits visible light but absorbs much of the ultraviolet, and brick transmits radio waves but not visible light.

The change of direction of a wave as it crosses the boundary between two substances at an angle to the normal. It is one of the effects a substance can have on a wave, alongside absorbing, transmitting and reflecting it.

concepts.term: Difference in velocity as the cause of refraction
concepts.def: Some effects, for example refraction, are due to the difference in velocity of the waves in different substances. If a wave had the same velocity in both substances it would cross the boundary without changing direction, however steep the angle.

concepts.term: What changes and what does not at a boundary
concepts.def: The frequency of a wave is set by its source and does not change when the wave enters a new substance. The velocity does change, so the wavelength must change with it: a wave that slows down has a shorter wavelength in the new substance.

A construction line drawn at right angles to the boundary at the exact point where the ray meets it, usually shown dashed. Every angle in a refraction ray diagram is measured from the normal, never from the boundary itself.

concepts.term: Angle of incidence and angle of refraction
concepts.def: The angle of incidence is the angle between the incident ray and the normal. The angle of refraction is the angle between the refracted ray and the normal, measured on the far side of the boundary.

concepts.term: Constructing a ray diagram for refraction
concepts.def: Draw the boundary, add the dashed normal where the ray strikes it, draw the incident ray with an arrow towards the boundary, then draw the refracted ray continuing from that same point with an arrow away from it. A ray entering a substance in which it travels more slowly bends towards the normal; one entering a substance in which it travels faster bends away from the normal; a ray along the normal is not deviated.

A line joining points of a wave that are all in phase with one another, for example all the crests. Wave fronts are drawn at right angles to the direction in which the wave travels, and the spacing between them is the wavelength.

concepts.term: Explaining refraction with a wave front diagram
concepts.def: When wave fronts meet a boundary at an angle, one end of each front crosses into the new medium before the other end does. If the wave travels more slowly in the new medium that end is held back while the rest of the front is still moving at the old speed, so the front pivots and the whole wave changes direction. The fronts also become closer together, because the wavelength falls with the speed.

Electromagnetic radiation emitted by all objects because of their temperature, and the radiation investigated in Required practical activity 10. A hotter object emits infrared at a greater rate than a cooler one.

concepts.term: How the nature of a surface affects infrared
concepts.def: A matt black surface is the best absorber of infrared radiation and also the best emitter of it. A shiny, silvered or pale surface is a poor absorber and a poor emitter, and reflects most of the infrared that reaches it. A good absorber is always a good emitter.

A hollow metal cube whose four vertical faces are given different surfaces, for example matt black, matt white, shiny silver and dull grey. Filling it with hot water puts every face at the same temperature, so any difference in the infrared detected must be caused by the nature of the surface.

concepts.term: Control variables in Required practical activity 10
concepts.def: The nature of the surface is the independent variable, so everything else must be kept the same: the temperature of the water, the distance from the surface to the detector, the orientation of the detector and the time allowed before each reading is taken. Changing any of these alongside the surface makes the comparison invalid.

mcqs.q: A sheet of window glass lets almost all of the visible light reaching it pass through, but it absorbs most of the ultraviolet. What does this show?
options: Whether a substance absorbs or transmits a wave can depend on the wavelength of that wave.
A material that looks clear to the eye must be transmitting every wave reaching it.
Ultraviolet is absorbed by every substance it meets, whatever that substance is.
Any wave the glass does not transmit must be completely absorbed by it.
mcqs.explain: Different substances may absorb, transmit, refract or reflect electromagnetic waves in ways that vary with wavelength, and one substance treating two wavelengths differently is exactly that.

mcqs.q: Which statement about how substances behave towards electromagnetic waves is correct?
options: A substance that fails to transmit a wave must have absorbed the whole of it.
One substance can reflect one wavelength but absorb a different one.
A wave behaves in just the same way in every substance it meets.
A clear substance will transmit every wavelength reaching it.
mcqs.explain: This is what the specification means by behaviour varying with wavelength: a single substance treats different wavelengths differently.

mcqs.q: Radio waves from a distant transmitter pass easily through the brick walls of a house, but visible light from outside does not. Which explanation is best?
options: Radio waves carry far more energy than light, so they force a way through brick.
Brick is not transparent, so no electromagnetic wave at all can cross it.
The brick transmits radio waves but reflects and absorbs the light.
The light is not transmitted, so the wall absorbs every bit of it.
mcqs.explain: The same substance behaves differently towards different wavelengths, which is precisely the variation with wavelength the specification describes.

mcqs.q: A water wave crosses from deep water into shallow water at an angle to the boundary and changes direction. What causes the change of direction?
options: The wave bounces off the edge of the shallow part and is pushed aside.
The shallow water blocks part of the wave, so the rest swings round.
The two depths pull on the wave with different sideways forces.
The wave has a different velocity in the shallower water.
mcqs.explain: Some effects, for example refraction, are due to the difference in velocity of the waves in different substances.

mcqs.q: Light travelling through air enters a glass block, where it travels more slowly. Its frequency does not change. What happens to its wavelength?
options: It stays the same, because the wavelength is fixed by the lamp producing it.
It gets shorter, because the velocity falls while the frequency stays the same.
It gets longer, because a slower wave needs more time for each cycle.
It stays the same, because light has one fixed speed in everything.
mcqs.explain: With the velocity smaller and the frequency unchanged, the wavelength must fall, so the wave fronts sit closer together in the glass.

mcqs.q: A student is drawing a ray diagram for light passing from air into a glass block. Where should the angle of incidence be measured?
options: Between the incoming ray and the flat surface of the glass block itself.
Between the incoming ray and the refracted ray inside the block.
Between the incoming ray and the normal drawn at the point it enters.
Between the refracted ray and the flat surface of the block.
mcqs.explain: The normal is the dashed line at right angles to the boundary at the point of entry, and both angles are measured from it.

mcqs.q: A ray of light travels from air into a glass block along the normal, so the angle of incidence is 0°. What should the ray diagram show?
options: The ray bends towards the normal as it enters, then bends back as it leaves.
The ray bends away from the normal as soon as it crosses into the glass.
The ray bends sideways as soon as it enters the glass block.
The ray carries straight on through the block without changing course.
mcqs.explain: Along the normal every part of the wave front crosses the boundary at the same instant, so the wave slows but is not deviated.

mcqs.q: In a wave front diagram, what does each drawn line represent?
options: A line joining points of the wave that are all in phase.
A line drawn parallel to the direction the wave is travelling.
A line whose spacing is the same in every medium it enters.
A line that is spaced more widely wherever the wave moves slower.
mcqs.explain: A wave front joins points in phase, such as all the crests, and it lies at right angles to the direction of travel.

mcqs.q: A wave front diagram shows plane wave fronts meeting a boundary at an angle. The wave travels more slowly in the second medium. Why do the fronts change direction?
options: The whole of each front slows down at the very same instant it crosses.
The fronts turn because the ray drawn through them is refracted there.
One end of each front enters the slower medium first and is held back, so it pivots.
The fronts spread further apart in the slower medium, and that turns them.
mcqs.explain: While one end is slowed and the other is still at the original speed the front swings round, which is the wave front explanation of refraction.

mcqs.q: In Required practical activity 10 a Leslie cube is filled with hot water. An infrared detector is placed the same distance from each vertical face in turn. Which face gives the highest reading?
options: All four read the same, because the water behind each face is at one temperature.
The shiny silver face, because polished metal gives out infrared best.
The matt white face, because pale surfaces give out the most radiation.
The matt black face, because matt black is the best emitter of infrared.
mcqs.explain: A good absorber is also a good emitter, so the matt black face radiates most strongly at that temperature.

mcqs.q: A student compares the infrared radiation emitted by the four faces of a Leslie cube. Which change would most improve the investigation?
options: Keep the detector the same distance from every face when reading it.
Move the detector closer to the darker faces so their readings are clearer.
Take the reading from each of the faces at a different water temperature.
Use a separate metal cube for each of the four surfaces tested.
mcqs.explain: Distance is a control variable: the reading falls as the detector is moved away, so it must be fixed if only the surface is to change.

mcqs.q: Four identical cans are painted matt black, matt white, shiny silver and dull grey. Each is filled with cold water and placed the same distance from a radiant heater. Which can's water warms fastest?
options: The shiny silver can, because a polished metal surface takes radiation in best.
The matt black can, because it is the best absorber of infrared.
All four cans equally, because the heater is the same distance away.
The dull grey can, because a metal surface draws radiation in fastest.
mcqs.explain: Matt black is the best absorber, so it takes in radiation from the heater at the greatest rate and warms fastest.

mcqs.q: A ray of light travels through air and strikes the flat surface of a glass block at an angle to the normal. Light travels more slowly in glass than in air. Which statement correctly describes the refracted ray inside the glass?
options: It bends towards the normal, because it slows down in the glass.
It bends away from the normal as it enters the glass.
It carries straight on undeviated, changing only its speed.
It reflects off the surface without entering the glass at all.
mcqs.explain: Air into glass is a change to a slower medium, and a ray slowing at an angled boundary bends towards the normal.
